# 2 Samuel Chapter 11 — The LOGOS Bible (Formal)
**Translator:** LOGOS | **Source:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folios 179v–180r | **Source Image:** source-texts/hebrew-OT/2SA_011_page_001.jpg, 2SA_011_page_002.jpg

---

**1** In the spring of the year, at the time when kings go out to battle, David sent Joab and his servants with him and all Israel, and they ravaged the Ammonites and besieged Rabbah. But David remained in Jerusalem.

**2** It happened one evening that David arose from his bed and walked about on the roof of the king's house. And from the roof he saw a woman bathing, and the woman was very beautiful.

**3** David sent and inquired about the woman. And one said, "Is this not Bathsheba, the daughter of Eliam, the wife of Uriah the Hittite?"

**4** David sent messengers and took her, and she came to him, and he lay with her — now she had been purifying herself from her uncleanness — and she returned to her house.

**5** The woman conceived, and she sent and told David, "I am pregnant."

**6** So David sent word to Joab: "Send me Uriah the Hittite." And Joab sent Uriah to David.

**7** When Uriah came to him, David asked about the welfare of Joab, the welfare of the army, and the welfare of the war.

**8** Then David said to Uriah, "Go down to your house and wash your feet." Uriah went out of the king's house, and a gift from the king followed him.

**9** But Uriah lay down at the entrance of the king's house with all the servants of his lord, and did not go down to his house.

**10** When they told David, "Uriah did not go down to his house," David said to Uriah, "Have you not come from a journey? Why did you not go down to your house?"

**11** Uriah said to David, "The ark and Israel and Judah dwell in booths, and my lord Joab and the servants of my lord are camped in the open field. Shall I then go to my house to eat and to drink and to lie with my wife? As you live, and as your soul lives, I will not do this thing."

**12** David said to Uriah, "Remain here today also, and tomorrow I will send you back." So Uriah remained in Jerusalem that day and the next.

**13** David invited him, and he ate in his presence and drank, and David made him drunk. And in the evening Uriah went out to lie on his bed among the servants of his lord, but he did not go down to his house.

**14** In the morning David wrote a letter to Joab and sent it by the hand of Uriah.

**15** In the letter he wrote, "Set Uriah in the forefront of the fiercest fighting, then draw back from him, that he may be struck down and die."

**16** And as Joab was besieging the city, he assigned Uriah to the place where he knew the enemy's strongest warriors were.

**17** The men of the city came out and fought with Joab, and some of the servants of David among the people fell. Uriah the Hittite also died.

**18** Then Joab sent and reported to David all the events of the war.

**19** He instructed the messenger, saying, "When you have finished telling the king all the events of the war,

**20** if the king's anger rises and he says to you, 'Why did you approach so near to the city to fight? Did you not know that they would shoot from the wall?

**21** Who struck Abimelech the son of Jerubbesheth? Did not a woman throw an upper millstone on him from the wall, so that he died at Thebez? Why did you approach the wall?' — then you shall say, 'Your servant Uriah the Hittite is dead also.'"

**22** So the messenger went and came and told David all that Joab had sent him to tell.

**23** The messenger said to David, "The men prevailed against us and came out to us in the field, but we drove them back to the entrance of the gate.

**24** Then the archers shot at your servants from the wall. Some of the king's servants are dead, and your servant Uriah the Hittite is dead also."

**25** David said to the messenger, "Thus you shall say to Joab: 'Do not let this matter trouble you, for the sword devours now one and now another. Strengthen your assault against the city and overthrow it.' And encourage him."

**26** When the wife of Uriah heard that Uriah her husband was dead, she mourned for her husband.

**27** When the time of mourning was over, David sent and brought her to his house, and she became his wife and bore him a son. But the thing that David had done was evil in the eyes of the LORD.

---
## LOGOS Translation Notes

**Verse 1 — "at the time when kings go out":** The Hebrew *le-et tset ha-melakhim* establishes the chapter's moral framework in its opening clause. The time is specified: it is the season when kings lead armies. David sends others. The narrator makes no explicit judgment; the structure does the work.

**Verse 4 — parenthetical clause:** The phrase "now she had been purifying herself from her uncleanness" (*ve-hi mitqaddeshet mitum'atah*) is a temporal-circumstantial clause. Its narrative function is twofold: (1) it explains why Bathsheba was bathing (ritual purification after menstruation), and (2) it eliminates any possibility that the child could be Uriah's.

**Verse 11 — Uriah's oath:** The soldier's speech is a masterpiece of unwitting irony. Every word of his loyalty condemns the king. "As you live, and as your soul lives" — Uriah swears by the life of the man who is plotting to take his. The triple refusal (to eat, drink, and lie with his wife) mirrors what David has done in excess.

**Verse 15 — the letter:** David writes the death warrant and sends it by the hand of the condemned man. This is one of the most chilling details in biblical narrative. The Hebrew Bible rarely comments on the inner states of characters; here, the silence about Uriah's thoughts as he carries the sealed letter is itself an act of narrative art.

**Verse 25 — "the sword devours":** David's proverb reduces murder to military fortune. The verb *tokhal* (devours/consumes) personifies the sword as an indiscriminate eater. David's instruction to "encourage" Joab (*chazzqehu*) is the final perversion — the language of covenant loyalty used to cover an assassination.

**Verse 27 — the closing verdict:** "But the thing that David had done was evil in the eyes of the LORD." The narrator has withheld all moral commentary throughout the chapter. This single sentence breaks the silence and sets up the confrontation with Nathan in chapter 12.

**Consistent terms:** the LORD (YHWH), soul (*nephesh*), Hittite (Chitti).

*— LOGOS*
